framing.title: The debate in one paragraph
framing.text: Bart Ehrman and Daniel Wallace, the two best-known voices on either side, agree on most of the data: there are hundreds of thousands of variants, most are trivial, a few matter, and the earliest centuries are thinly attested. They disagree about what follows. Ehrman stresses that we lack the originals and early copies and that scribes sometimes changed the text on purpose; Wallace stresses that the wealth of witnesses lets us recover the original wording in almost every place, and that no core belief rests on a disputed passage.

telephone.intro: The simulator is a teaching model, not a reconstruction method. Its limits are real.

points.text: The simulation treats every scribe's errors as independent. Real scribes copied from exemplars inside text families and often mixed readings from several exemplars, so shared mistakes travel together and there are fewer truly independent lines than the tree suggests.
points.reply: Mixture is real, and it is the reason the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method was built; applied to the whole tradition it still yields a stable initial text at almost every point of variation.

points.text: The earliest generations, before about 150 AD, have almost no surviving witnesses. The tree is thinnest exactly where it matters most, and changes made then could have spread to every surviving line.
points.reply: Second- and third-century papyri, early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic) and quotations by early writers are independent windows into that period, and they largely agree with the later text.

points.text: Majority vote is not how textual criticism works. Editors weigh witnesses by age, family and coherence, and sometimes follow a minority reading, so a count of copies can mislead.
points.reply: Agreed, and real methods do better than the simulator: weighting early, independent witnesses is how editors can correct even a majority error.

points.text: Some changes were deliberate, made to sharpen doctrine or harmonize the Gospels, and deliberate changes are more likely to be copied than random slips.
points.reply: The deliberate changes that have been documented are detectable because other lines kept the unaltered reading, and none of them is the sole basis for a core belief.

timeline.intro: The chart shows access to earlier witnesses growing over time. What it does not show matters too.

points.text: Count is not the same as reliability. Most of the roughly 5,800 manuscripts are medieval, copied a thousand years or more after the originals, and many of them descend from a few late exemplars.
points.reply: The argument rests on the early witnesses, not the medieval bulk; what the timeline shows is the earliest known copy moving back by more than a thousand years since 1516.

points.text: Papyrus dates rest on handwriting comparison, which is less precise than often presented. P52, usually dated about 125–175, could be later.
points.reply: Specialists who re-examined the early papyri with that critique in view still date P52 to about 125–175, and even the later datings keep the papyri far closer than anything known in 1611.

points.text: The manuscript counts for other ancient authors come from catalogues of uneven date and change as they are revised; the older tallies repeated for decades in popular apologetics were substantially off.
points.reply: Updated tallies still put the New Testament far ahead on both count and gap; the comparison survives even generous corrections to the classical figures.

points.text: The figure of about 5,800 counts every catalogued item, including fragments of a few verses and lectionaries that reorder the text for reading in church.
points.reply: True; continuous-text manuscripts alone number over 3,300 (papyri, majuscules and minuscules in the 2013 tally), and several of the 'fragments' are the oldest witnesses.

p66.intro: P66 is an early and substantial witness to John. How early, and how careful, are debated.

points.text: P66 is usually dated about 200 AD, but the date rests on handwriting, and one detailed study argues a 4th-century date is possible.
points.reply: Most papyrologists still place it around 200–250, and even a 4th-century date would leave it among the earliest near-complete copies of John.

points.text: Its scribe made hundreds of mistakes and corrections, including readings found nowhere else, which shows how easily an early copy could go wrong.
points.reply: Most corrections bring the text back into line with the wider tradition, which shows the copy was checked against another exemplar soon after it was made.

variants.intro: The numbers here are real, and some of them are large.

points.text: There are hundreds of thousands of textual variants, more than there are words in the New Testament. A careful recent estimate puts the number of non-spelling variants alone around half a million.
points.reply: Both sides accept the number; the question is what kind of variants they are, and the great majority are spelling, word order and similar slips that do not change the sense.

points.text: Some variants are theologically loaded: the long ending of Mark, the woman caught in adultery, and the Johannine Comma were read as Scripture for centuries, and some changes appear to be motivated by doctrinal debate.
points.reply: Those passages are marked in every modern Bible, which is the point of this module, and no doctrine depends on them alone.

points.text: The category percentages are estimates from popular summaries, not a published count of every variant by type.
points.reply: The shares are rough, but every meaningful and viable variant is printed in the critical apparatus, so the claim can be checked passage by passage.

names.intro: The name statistics are suggestive. The sample is small and the method has critics.

points.text: The Gospels and Acts name only dozens of Palestinian Jews (79 men and 18 women in the tally used here), so each percentage moves several points with a single name, and a rough fit is easy to get by chance.
points.reply: The pattern that matters most is specific rather than statistical: common names get a qualifier and rare ones don't, which a small sample shows clearly.

points.text: Bauckham's counts and his choice of which names to include have been questioned, and his printed shares do not all match his own tables (this page shows both).
points.reply: The recomputed shares differ in detail but keep the same shape: the Gospels' most common names are the population's most common names.

points.text: A good match shows that the traditions came from first-century Palestine. It does not show that eyewitnesses wrote the Gospels, and later writers with access to Palestinian tradition could match it too.
points.reply: Agreed; the modest claim is that the traditions stayed close to their Palestinian sources, which later gospels written elsewhere mostly do not.

coincidences.intro: Undesigned coincidences are a cumulative argument, and each link can be challenged.

points.text: Some coincidences can be explained by literary dependence: Matthew and Luke used Mark, so a detail one explains may simply have been copied and adjusted.
points.reply: The strongest cases cross from the Synoptics to John, where copying is least likely, and dependence does not explain why the source lacks the detail that explains its own story.

points.text: There is a selection effect: we notice the pieces that fit and pass over the many details that do not interlock or that appear to conflict.
points.reply: The argument needs the fits to be more frequent than chance or invention would produce, and the apocryphal gospels, where such interlocks are rare, provide the comparison.

points.text: At most, interlocking details show that the writers had access to real information. They do not show that every detail in the Gospels is historical.
points.reply: That is the claim being made: interlocking detail is the fingerprint of independent access to the same events, which is what a reliable report looks like.
